terms.gloss: close-fitting cap or hat, originally of felt
terms.comment: Applied here to modern caps without claiming every modern shape was ancient. A container’s cap or lid is operculum, operculī n., not this headwear noun.

phrases.latin: Pilleum lāneum indue, nē aurēs algeant.
phrases.english: Put your woolly hat on, so your ears don’t get cold.
Put on your party hat: the party’s starting!

phrases.latin: Synthesibus dum gaudet eques dominusque senātor dumque decent nostrum pillea sūmpta Jovem
phrases.english: while the knight and the lordly senator enjoy their party clothes, and the cap he has put on becomes our Jupiter

phrases.latin: Ūnctīs falciferī senis diēbus, rēgnātor quibus inperat fritillus, versū lūdere nōn labōriōsō permittis, putō, pilleāta Rōma.
phrases.english: On the feast days of the old god with the sickle, when the dice-box is king, you let me play in easy verse, I think, Rome in your party caps.

pilleus.against: the single-l pīleus of Morgan–Owens s.v. hat: cap
pilleus.html: Traupman 116, 286, followed here; Lewis & Short’s headword is pilleus too.

sources: Lewis & Short: pilleus · Morgan–Owens: hat: cap · Lewis & Short: laneus · Lewis & Short: pilleatus
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 114, 116, 286.
